name: JPMorgan Chase

header.one_liner: The best-run US bank, earning a 20% return on tangible equity, priced at three times tangible book.
header.thesis: JPMorgan grew net interest income 13% and earned $5.57 a share in the September quarter, with equity trading up 49% and credit losses steady at 1.35% of loans. The franchise is the strongest in US banking; the question is whether 14.5x earnings and 3x tangible book leave room for a return above the cost of equity as rates and credit normalise.

base.eps_label: FY2026E diluted EPS excluding the $4.6B second-quarter gain on Visa shares: nine months $19.20 less about $1.30 for the gain, plus a fourth quarter near $5.60
base.rev_label: FY2026E managed net revenue ($B): nine months $159.5B less the $4.6B Visa gain, plus a fourth quarter near $50B

rev_cagr.why: Managed revenue grew 8% in the quarter: net interest income +13% on 10% loan growth, investment banking fees +13% and equity trading +49%. Some of that is unusually strong markets activity. The base case assumes about 4% a year as rates ease and trading normalises.
rev_cagr.source: JPMorgan Q3 2026 earnings release financial supplement

margin_end.why: Net income is about 31% of revenue this year, helped by low credit costs (net charge-offs 1.35% of loans) and strong fees. The base case assumes credit costs and expenses rise a little faster than revenue; the bear case is a credit cycle.

share_chg.why: Diluted shares fell 3% over the past year, but buybacks dropped to $1.1B in the third quarter from $8.3B a year earlier, under a new $50B program from 1 July 2026. The base case assumes about 2% a year.

exit_pe.why: JPMorgan trades at about 14.5x 2026 EPS and 3x tangible book, against 10x to 11x for Bank of America, Citigroup and Wells Fargo. The base case assumes a small de-rating as returns normalise; the premium to peers is earned but already wide.
exit_pe.source: Engine judgment; peer multiples from the Moat Monitor peer table

pillars.title: Net interest income is still rising
pillars.claim: NII grew 13% to $27.0B on 10% loan growth and 9% deposit growth.
pillars.test: Does NII hold as the Fed cuts?

pillars.title: Markets and banking fees are strong
pillars.claim: Equity markets revenue rose 49% and investment banking fees 13%; fixed income fell 4%.

evidence.t: Equity Markets $4,954M vs $3,331M; Fixed Income Markets $5,366M vs $5,613M

pillars.test: How much of the trading strength repeats?

pillars.title: Credit is steady
pillars.claim: Net charge-offs were 1.35% of loans and the allowance was flat; the provision was $2.7B.
pillars.test: Do card charge-offs rise as unemployment does?

pillars.title: Capital return slowed
pillars.claim: Buybacks fell to $1.1B in the quarter and CET1 eased to 13.9%; the dividend was raised 10% to $1.65.

evidence.t: Aggregate repurchases $1,057M vs $8,315M a year earlier

pillars.test: Do buybacks resume under the new $50B program?

variant.street: The market pays 14.5x earnings and 3x tangible book for the bank with the highest returns and the strongest franchise.
variant.ours: The premium is earned, but it leaves little room. With rates easing and credit costs at a low, our base case earnings grow slowly and the 12-month return falls short of the cost of equity.
variant.could_be_wrong: If capital rules ease and JPMorgan deploys its excess capital in buybacks, EPS can grow high single digits with no change in operations.
variant.would_change_mind: Buybacks back above $7B a quarter, or the stock nearer 2.5x tangible book.

moat.summary: Scale in deposits, cards, payments and investment banking; the lowest funding cost and highest returns among large US banks.
moat.detail: Rated from the latest 10-K and 10-Q; see the moat window for the sources of advantage.

lenses.eisman: Credit is the swing factor at a bank this size; check card charge-offs every quarter.

lenses.buffett: He admires the franchise and has said banks are worth buying at a sensible price to book.

review.basis: Q3 2026 earnings release financial supplement (quarter to 30 September 2026). Q4 reports in mid-January; this review refreshes after the print.
review.headline: The strongest US bank, earning about 20% on tangible equity. The premium to peers is deserved and already in the price.
review.model: JPMorgan takes deposits and lends them out (consumer, card, commercial), runs the largest US investment bank and trading business, and manages money for wealthy clients and institutions. It earns the spread on loans, plus fees.

how_it_earns.v: Chase branches, cards, mortgages and auto loans. Most of the deposits.
Advisory, underwriting, trading, payments and corporate lending.
Fees on client assets. Steady and growing.
The spread between loan and deposit rates. About half of revenue.

mix.note: Revenue by region from the 2025 10-K. JPMorgan's business segments are in the earnings supplement, summarised on this page.

review.position: The largest US bank by assets, deposits and market value, and the largest US investment bank by fees.

sources: Technology spend no rival can match
moat.threat: Regulation and the credit cycle, not competitors, set the limits.

what_numbers_say.d: Equity markets $5.0B; fixed income -4%; IB fees +13%.
$1.1B in Q3 vs $8.3B a year earlier; CET1 13.9%.

balance.read: Well capitalised: CET1 13.9% and a fortress balance sheet, with excess capital above requirements.

flags.evidence: A $4.6B net gain on Visa class C shares in the second quarter lifts nine-month EPS by about $1.30.
Noninterest expense +12% vs managed revenue +8% in the quarter.
Repurchases $1.1B in Q3 vs $6.7B in Q2 and $8.3B a year earlier.

base.story: Revenue grows about 4% a year, credit costs normalise slowly and buybacks continue at a moderate pace.

downside.story: A recession lifts card and commercial losses while rate cuts squeeze NII; the multiple falls toward 11x.

upside.story: Capital rules ease and excess capital is returned; trading stays strong and EPS grows high single digits.

risks.how: Card and consumer losses rise with unemployment; commercial real estate is a second pocket.
Deposit costs fall more slowly than loan yields when the Fed cuts.
Equity markets revenue rose 49%; a quieter market would cut fees.
Higher capital requirements would slow buybacks further.
Leadership succession at the top is a long-standing question for investors.

peer_read.why_premium: JPMorgan earns the highest returns on tangible equity among US universal banks and has the strongest deposit franchise.
peer_read.why_not: At 14x earnings it is about a third more expensive than Bank of America, Citigroup and Wells Fargo, which are improving faster from a lower base.
peer_read.peers_note: Banks are compared on P/E only; enterprise value and EBITDA are not meaningful for lenders.

questions: How much of the 20% return on tangible equity is cyclical?
Why did buybacks slow in the third quarter?
Is a one-third premium to peers too much?

arguments.label: Growth
arguments.text: Managed revenue grew 8% in the September quarter: net interest income +13% on 10% loan growth, equity trading +49%, investment banking fees +13%.

arguments.label: Moat
arguments.text: The lowest-cost deposit base and the largest card, payments and investment banking franchises in the US. Regulation and credit set the limits.

arguments.label: Profitability
arguments.text: Return on tangible equity of 20% in the quarter and 24% year to date, with net charge-offs at 1.35% of loans. Expenses grew 12%, faster than revenue.

arguments.label: Capital

thesis_long: JPMorgan is the strongest bank in the US. It has the cheapest deposits, the largest card and payments franchise and the top investment bank, and it is still growing: loans +10%, net interest income +13% and equity trading +49% in the September quarter. Return on tangible equity was 24% for the first nine months.

The question is what is left for a new buyer. At about 14.5x this year's earnings and 3x tangible book, the stock trades about a third above Bank of America, Citigroup and Wells Fargo. Earnings are flattered by low credit costs and strong trading, rate cuts will slow net interest income, expenses are growing faster than revenue, and buybacks dropped to $1.1B in the quarter.

We value JPMorgan on tangible book against what its equity earns, as banks are valued. Our base case grows revenue about 4% a year with slightly higher credit costs, which keeps return on tangible equity near 20%. Against the cost of equity that justifies about 3x tangible book, close to today’s multiple, so the 12-month return comes from book growth and dividends: above the cost of equity, but not by the margin an Overweight needs. We would turn positive if buybacks returned above $7B a quarter or the price fell nearer 2.5x tangible book.

upside_risks.how: Lower capital requirements would release excess capital for buybacks, lifting EPS growth without any change in operations.
Another year of record trading and a recovery in M&A would push earnings well above our base case.

dcf.label: EPS. Free cash flow is not meaningful for a bank, whose cash flows include deposits and loans

valuation.bvps_label: Tangible book value per share $112.64 at 30 September 2026 (third-quarter earnings release)
valuation.why: A bank is worth what its equity earns. The justified multiple of tangible book is (return on tangible equity less long-run growth) divided by (cost of equity less growth). Return on equity comes from our earnings path, book per share rolls forward a year with earnings, dividends and buybacks at today’s price, and growth is 4%, about the long-run growth of nominal US GDP.
valuation.note_exit: The 12-month target is set by return on equity against the cost of equity, so a dispute on the exit P/E changes the 3-year scenarios but not the target.
